## How our static-site releases work

Each release has two steps, and the order matters:

1. **Upload every new asset under a versioned name.** Each JS bundle, stylesheet, image and font gets a name that includes its version or content hash, for example `app.3f9c2a.js` instead of `app.js`. Nothing is overwritten.
2. **Switch the manifest to the new names.** The manifest (or the HTML entry point that references it) maps each logical asset to its current versioned file. Updating it is the single change that makes the release live.

### Why the upload comes before the switch

The manifest is the only thing that tells browsers which files to request. As soon as it points at the new names, browsers start fetching them.

If we switched first, there would be a window where the manifest points at files that don't exist yet. Any user who loaded the page in that window would get 404s for scripts or styles, which means a blank or broken page. On a slow or partially failed upload, that window could last minutes, or indefinitely.

Uploading first makes the release effectively atomic. Until the switch, users keep getting the complete old release. After the switch, every file the new manifest names is already in place. If the upload fails partway, we don't switch, and users never see the half-uploaded files.

### Why we keep the old assets

Switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already have the old one. Those users are still running the previous release and will keep requesting its files:

- **Open tabs.** A page loaded an hour ago still has the old manifest in memory.
- **Lazy loading.** Code-split chunks, route bundles and below-the-fold images are fetched only when the user navigates or scrolls, sometimes long after the initial page load.
- **Caches.** CDN edges, proxies, browser caches and service workers can serve the old HTML or manifest for a while after the release.

If we deleted the old files at release time, those users would hit 404s mid-session. Typically that shows up as a failed chunk load, a page that breaks when someone clicks a link, or missing styles. Keeping the old files lets every client finish using the release it started with.

Two other benefits follow from this:

- **Instant rollback.** The previous release is still fully uploaded, so rolling back means pointing the manifest at the old names again. Nothing needs to be rebuilt or re-uploaded.
- **Aggressive caching.** A versioned file never changes, so it can be cached as immutable with a long max-age. Only the manifest needs a short cache lifetime.

### Cleanup

Old assets aren't kept forever. Delete them only after they've gone unreferenced for longer than the longest realistic session plus the longest cache lifetime of the manifest and HTML.

The switch is then a single small change, so users get either the complete old release or the complete new one.

Keeping the old assets lets those sessions finish on the version they started with. They move to the new release on their next full load. Old assets can be cleaned up once no live session or cache could still reference them.

# How our static-site releases work

In short, we put every new file in place first, then flip one pointer to start using them, and we never delete the files the previous release depends on. This means no visitor ever requests a file that isn't there.

## The two steps

1. **Upload the new assets under versioned names.** Every build output (JS bundles, CSS, images, fonts) gets a name that is unique to its version, typically a content hash such as `app.3f9c2a.js`. Nothing already on the server is overwritten. At this point the new files exist, but no page references them, so visitors see no change.
2. **Switch the manifest.** The manifest (the HTML entry point or asset map that tells the browser which files to load) is updated to reference the new names. This is the moment the release goes live, and it is a single small change.

## Why the upload comes before the switch

The manifest is the only thing that tells browsers which files to fetch. If we switched it first, any browser that loaded the new manifest before the upload finished would request files that don't exist yet. The result would be 404s, unstyled pages, or a blank screen from a failed script load. A partial or failed upload would leave the site broken until someone intervened.

Uploading first makes the release effectively atomic:

- If the upload fails partway, nothing is affected. The live manifest still points at the old, complete set of files. We fix the problem and upload again.
- When the switch happens, every file the new manifest names is already present.
- Rollback is the same operation in reverse: point the manifest back at the previous version's names.

## Why we keep the old assets

When a visitor's browser loaded the previous manifest, it committed to that version's file names. It doesn't re-check the manifest on every request. A browser can still ask for old files after the switch in several ways:

- **Lazily loaded code.** Code-split bundles for routes or features are fetched only when the user navigates there. Someone who opened a tab an hour ago and clicks a new section will request an old chunk.
- **Long-lived tabs.** People leave tabs open for days.
- **Cached manifests.** Browsers, CDNs, proxies, and service workers may keep serving the old manifest until their cache expires. Some visitors receive the old version for a while after the switch.
- **Late-loading resources.** Fonts, images, and other assets referenced from old CSS or JS.

If we deleted the old files on release, all of these requests would fail. The user would see a broken page or a "failed to load chunk" error until they did a full reload. Because the names are versioned, old and new files never collide, so keeping both costs only storage.

Keeping old assets also makes rollback instant, because the previous version's files are still there to point back to.

## Related consequences

- **Caching.** A versioned file's content never changes under its name, so these assets can be cached for a long time as immutable. The manifest is the one thing that needs a short cache lifetime, because it is the part that changes.
- **Cleanup.** Old assets are removed only after a retention period that is comfortably longer than the manifest's cache lifetime plus a realistic tab lifetime. Never delete the assets of the release currently live or the one immediately before it.

## Rules of thumb

- Never overwrite a file in place. A new version means a new name.
- Never switch the manifest until the upload has completed and been verified.
- Never delete assets as part of a release. Cleanup is a separate step with its own retention window.
